title: Were Long Island’s Native communities independent, or part of a larger group?
summary: Each community governed itself, with its own Sachems, villages and homeland. There was no single Long Island Nation, but family, marriage, trade and related Algonquian languages connected communities to one another and to the Lenape and New England Algonquian Nations.
content:
Asked by Jody through Ask a question on November 3, 2026.

“Were all the groups (Nissequogues, Canarsies, Matinecocks, etc.) all independent or part of a larger group (Montauk, Lenape, etc.)?”

Short answer

Each community governed itself. The Nissequogue, Canarsie, Matinecock, Montaukett and other communities each had their own Sachems, villages and homelands. There was no single Long Island Nation, and the Montaukett did not rule the others.1

They were still closely connected through family, marriage, trade, diplomacy and related Algonquian languages.1 2

Connections to the west and east

All of Long Island’s Native languages are Algonquian. Much of western Long Island, including the Canarsie and Rockaway, had close Munsee (Lenape) language and family ties reaching Manhattan, Staten Island and New Jersey. See Western Long Island Native Communities.2

In the east, the Montaukett and Shinnecock spoke a language closely related to Mohegan-Pequot, and wampum trade and marriages tied them to Algonquian Nations across Long Island Sound. The Mohegan minister Samson Occom married Mary Fowler, a Montaukett woman, at Montauk, and in 1775 David Fowler led Montaukett families to the new Brothertown community in central New York.2 3

Sharing a language or family ties with the Lenape or the Pequot meant close relationships, not belonging to one government.

Two common myths

One Grand Sachem ruled the island. English colonists promoted the Montaukett Sachem Wyandanch as “Grand Sachem” and sought his approval for land sales across Long Island. In 1665, New York’s first English governor, Richard Nicolls, declared there was no longer any Grand Sachem and that every Sachem would keep authority over his own people.1 4

Long Island had exactly 13 tribes. Historian Silas Wood popularized that list in 1824, building it from names in colonial deeds. Many of those names describe places or local communities rather than Nations with fixed borders. See The Myth of the Thirteen Tribes.1 5

Still here today

The Shinnecock and Unkechaug Nations keep their own land bases and governments, and Montaukett, Matinecock, Setalcott and other communities continue through families, leadership and cultural work. See Native Communities and the “Thirteen Tribes” Model.
